Endocrinology · published research

Radiation-induced thyroid dysfunction

Summary of the Evidence

One Korean publication combined an experiment in irradiated human thyroid follicular cells with an ionizing-radiation mouse model. These are linked components of one paper, not two independent publications or clinical studies. No patient trial or separate replication was identified for this category (Yoo et al. 2021).

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical study in people receiving radiation therapy was identified. The use of a human-derived thyroid cell line does not count as a human treatment study.

Animal evidence

In irradiated mice, 850-nm LED exposure was reported to restore proliferation in thyroid follicular tissue and improve measured thyroid-associated markers, including cAMP, thyroglobulin, TSH, T3, and T4. This is a favorable result in one mouse model, but it does not show that PBM prevents or reverses thyroid dysfunction in patients or that light exposure near irradiated tissue is oncologically safe (Yoo et al. 2021).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

In irradiated N-Thy-3.1 human thyroid cells, PBM improved survival and proliferation and affected p53, retinoblastoma-protein, cAMP, and thyroglobulin measures. The study tested 2, 5, and 10 J/cm²; the authors identified 2 J/cm² as the most effective tested exposure for the reported cell-cycle outcome. These cell results come from the same publication as the mouse experiment (Yoo et al. 2021).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study used an 850-nm LED array. Cultured cells received 2, 5, or 10 J/cm², while the mouse protocol used 120 J/cm². The cell and animal doses are not interchangeable, and one external mouse exposure does not define a dose, schedule, tissue penetration, or safety profile for people receiving radiotherapy.

Interpretation

The study provides a favorable preclinical signal for recovery of irradiated thyroid cells and thyroid-associated markers. Certainty remains very low because the evidence comes from one linked laboratory-and-animal publication without clinical outcomes or independent replication. Clinical effectiveness, durability, and tumor-related safety remain unanswered.

Publications and records

1 publication

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Thyroid-cell proliferation and thyroid-marker recovery after radiation in preclinical models: very low certainty. The evidence comes from one linked cell-and-mouse publication without patient outcomes or independent replication.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

One publication combined irradiated human thyroid cells with an ionizing-radiation mouse model and reported recovery of proliferation and several thyroid-associated markers after 850-nm LED exposure. The two model components are not independent replications, and no patient outcomes were measured. Clinical effectiveness, durability, and safety during cancer radiotherapy therefore remain unknown, supporting very low certainty.
